core: Definition of social engineering as human-targeted manipulation (attributed to NIST SP 800-63-4 via the CSRC glossary)
Why attackers target people: technical systems carry strong defenses, so the human layer becomes the path of least resistance

Psychological levers: authority, urgency, fear, helpfulness

claims.claim: Social engineering deceives an individual into revealing sensitive information, obtaining unauthorized access, or committing fraud by building confidence and trust rather than breaking a technical defense (NIST SP 800-63-4 definition, collected in the NIST CSRC glossary).

Social engineering relies heavily on human interaction to influence an individual to violate security protocol and divulge confidential information; such attacks are committed via phone, in person, or online.
Attackers favor social engineering because reaching systems through technical controls such as firewalls and antivirus is difficult, while manipulating a person avoids that work.
Pretexting is a technique in which the attacker invents a fabricated situation and poses as the person entitled to resolve it.
Baiting is a technique that offers a tempting lure — such as a free download or a dropped USB drive — so that the victim's action on the offer compromises security.
Tailgating is a technique in which an unauthorized person follows an authorized person through a door or access point the attacker could not open alone.
Quid pro quo is a technique that dangles a desirable good or service in exchange for the victim's sensitive information or access.
Social engineering attacks apply psychological levers — posing as an authority, inducing fear or urgency, and appealing to helpfulness or curiosity — to drive victims to act against their interests.

A core defense practice is to verify identity through an independent channel — contact the organization at a phone number or website you know is real, not the one provided in the message — and layered protections such as multi-factor authentication limit the damage when credentials leak.
Anyone can be manipulated; awareness and careful habits reduce the odds of falling for social engineering but cannot guarantee protection.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Relationship between social engineering and phishing
positions: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 describes phishing as the online, email-based form of social engineering
Some vendor sources treat phishing and social engineering as parallel threat categories
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats social engineering as the broader category of human-targeted manipulation and phishing as its message-based form; phishing is owned by a sibling topic and referenced only.

positions: IBM describes both in-person following through a door and digital piggybacking on an unattended session
Most consumer and awareness guidance focuses on the physical form
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes the physical form (following an authorized person through a door), which is the concept named in the topic brief; the digital variant is not covered.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary — social engineering
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Computer Security Resource Center
sourceRecords.license: U.S. federal government work; not subject to copyright in the United States
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. The glossary entry collects attributed definitions: NIST SP 800-63-4 / SP 800-63A-4 define social engineering as the act of deceiving an individual into revealing sensitive information, obtaining unauthorized access, or committing fraud by associating with the individual to gain confidence and trust; CNSSI 4009-2015 / NIST SP 800-82r3 define it as an attempt to trick someone into revealing information (e.g., a password) that can be used to attack systems or networks; NIST SP 800-115 offers a similar tricking definition. Used as the attributed working definition in the lesson. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Special Publication 800-12 Revision 1: An Introduction to Information Security
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. Government work; not subject to copyright in the United States
sourceRecords.notes: Registered id reused with an identical URL. The PDF text layer was read directly (nvlpubs.nist.gov) on 2026-08-21. Section 4.2.2: social engineering, in the context of information security, is a technique that relies heavily on human interaction to influence an individual to violate security protocol and encourages the individual to divulge confidential information; attacks are commonly committed via phone or online, with phone attacks described as the most basic; the online email-based form is phishing; social media is used to gather contact information that enables social engineering. Section 7.3.2: social engineering involves deceiving users or administrators into divulging information about systems, including their passwords. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is social engineering? (IBM Security explainer)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21; reputable vendor explainer used as a secondary source. Supports: social engineering as psychological manipulation of people rather than exploitation of technical vulnerabilities (sometimes called 'human hacking'); attackers favor it because it avoids the difficult technical work of bypassing firewalls, antivirus, and other controls; the technique families — baiting (tempting lures such as free downloads or dropped USB drives), tailgating (following an authorized person through an access point), pretexting (inventing a fake situation and posing as the person to resolve it), quid pro quo (dangling a desirable good or service in exchange for information); the psychological levers (posing as a trusted brand, posing as an authority figure, inducing fear or urgency, appealing to helpfulness or curiosity); and the difficulty of prevention because manipulation targets psychology. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
